stem: Which cereal is grown in Zimbabwe mainly as an irrigated winter crop?

options.content: Wheat
options.rationale: Correct: planted in late April to May and harvested before the rains.

options.content: Pearl millet
options.rationale: Pearl millet is a rain-fed summer crop of dry regions.

options.content: Sorghum
options.rationale: Sorghum is a rain-fed summer crop.

options.content: Finger millet
options.rationale: Finger millet is a rain-fed summer crop.

explanation: Wheat needs cool weather and dry conditions at harvest, so it is grown in winter under irrigation.

stem: How does the waxy bloom on sorghum leaves help the crop in dry regions?

options.content: It reduces water loss from the leaves
options.rationale: Correct: the wax cuts transpiration from the surface.

options.content: It increases the rate of photosynthesis at night
options.rationale: Photosynthesis needs light; wax has no such role.

options.content: It allows the leaves to absorb rain directly
options.rationale: Leaves do not take up much water; the wax repels it.

options.content: It attracts bees for pollination
options.rationale: Sorghum is mostly self-pollinated and wind-pollinated.

explanation: The waxy layer reflects sunlight and reduces water loss, one of several drought-tolerance features.

stem: Why do farmers grow brown, high-tannin sorghum in areas with many quelea birds?

options.content: Brown grain ripens at night when birds sleep
options.rationale: Grain ripening has nothing to do with night.

options.content: High-tannin sorghum has no grain at all
options.rationale: It produces grain; birds simply eat less of it.

options.content: The brown colour cannot be seen by birds
options.rationale: Birds see brown grain perfectly well.

options.content: Birds find the bitter grain less palatable
options.rationale: Correct: tannins make the grain less attractive to birds.

explanation: Tannins give an astringent taste; bird-resistant sorghums lose less grain but are less preferred for food.

stem: A farmer in natural region V has deep sandy soil and very unreliable rain. Which cereal is the most suitable?

options.content: Wheat
options.rationale: Wheat needs winter irrigation, not dryland conditions.

options.content: A late-maturing maize hybrid
options.rationale: Long-season maize would often fail in region V.

options.content: Pearl millet
options.rationale: Correct: the most drought- and heat-tolerant cereal, suited to sandy soils.

options.content: Rice
options.rationale: Rice needs plenty of water.

explanation: Pearl millet yields where maize fails: it tolerates heat, sandy infertile soils and dry spells.
hints: Which cereal tolerates heat, sand and drought best?

stem: Why is wheat in Zimbabwe planted in late April to May rather than in November?

options.content: It needs the heavy summer rains to germinate
options.rationale: Wheat is irrigated; summer rains would harm it at harvest.

options.content: It needs cool weather to grow and must be harvested before the rains
options.rationale: Correct: summer heat and rain at harvest would spoil it.

options.content: Wheat grain is damaged by cool temperatures
options.rationale: Wheat grows best in cool conditions.

options.content: Irrigation water from dams is only available during the rainy season
options.rationale: Irrigation lets wheat grow in the dry season.

explanation: Planting in late April to May gives cool growing conditions and a dry harvest in September to October.
hints: Think about temperature during growth and weather at harvest.

stem: Which practice helps control witchweed in a sorghum field?

options.content: Growing sorghum on the same land every year
options.rationale: Continuous sorghum builds up witchweed seed.

options.content: Leaving the soil infertile and unmanured
options.rationale: Witchweed is worst on poor soil; manure and nitrogen help.

options.content: Pulling the witchweed before it flowers
options.rationale: Correct: it stops new seed from being added to the soil.

options.content: Ploughing the witchweed seed deeper every year
options.rationale: Witchweed seed lives for years and is not destroyed by ploughing.

explanation: Witchweed produces huge numbers of long-lived seeds; prevent seeding, rotate with non-host crops and improve fertility.
hints: How does witchweed spread from season to season?

stem: Which small grain is best known for keeping for several years in store with little insect damage?

options.content: Maize
options.rationale: Maize is attacked by weevils and the larger grain borer.

options.content: Finger millet
options.rationale: Correct: its small, hard grain stores very well.

options.content: Wheat
options.rationale: Wheat stores well only if dry, and is not the small grain intended.

options.content: Groundnuts
options.rationale: Groundnuts are a legume, not a small grain.

explanation: Finger millet (rapoko) has long been kept as a famine reserve because it stores so well.

stem: In a season with a three-week dry spell at flowering, sorghum yielded more than maize on the same farm. Which explanation is best?

options.content: Sorghum does not need any water during flowering
options.rationale: All crops need water; sorghum tolerates shortage better.

options.content: Maize roots are deeper, so they dried out faster
options.rationale: Sorghum has the more extensive root system.

options.content: The sorghum must have been irrigated by the farmer during the dry spell
options.rationale: Nothing in the question suggests irrigation.

options.content: Sorghum can pause growth in drought and recover; maize fails at tasselling
options.rationale: Correct: maize is most sensitive to water stress at flowering.

explanation: Sorghum's roots, waxy leaves, leaf rolling and ability to recover after drought explain its better yield.
hints: When is maize most sensitive to drought?

stem: Sorghum and millets suit natural regions IV and V better than maize does.
explanation: True. They tolerate the low, unreliable rainfall of regions IV and V.

stem: Cattle can safely graze very young sorghum regrowth at any time.
explanation: False. Young or stressed sorghum can release prussic acid (hydrogen cyanide) in the rumen and poison livestock.

stem: Match each crop with the description that fits it best.

right.content: Waxy leaves; red, brown or white grain used for malt
Drilled in close rows in winter under irrigation
Candle-like heads; tolerates hot, sandy, dry land
Small seeds needing a fine seedbed; excellent storage

explanation: Each cereal has distinctive features and conditions.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Side shoots that grow from the base of a wheat plant are called {{blank:a}}, and the small bird that damages ripening sorghum in large flocks is the red-billed {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Tillers carry extra ears; quelea flocks can strip fields of small grains.

stem: Wheat is sown at 120 kg/ha on 2.4 ha. Calculate the mass of seed needed, in kg.
explanation: 120 × 2.4 = 288 kg of seed (28.8 or 2,880 come from slipping a decimal point).
workedSolution: 1. 120 × 2.4 = 288 kg of seed (28.8 or 2,880 come from slipping a decimal point).

stem: Each irrigation of a 1.5 ha wheat field applies 50 mm of water. Calculate the volume of water per irrigation in m³. (1 mm of water over 1 m² is 1 L; 1 m³ = 1,000 L.)
explanation: 1.5 ha = 15,000 m²; 15,000 × 50 = 750,000 L = 750 m³. Using 1.5 × 50 = 75 forgets to convert hectares to square metres.

stem: Sorghum is thinned to 12 cm within rows 90 cm apart. Calculate the plant population per hectare, to the nearest whole plant.
Name the poisonous substance that young sorghum plants can release in the stomach of grazing cattle.
explanation: **Prussic acid** (hydrogen cyanide).

stem: Explain **two** features that make sorghum more drought tolerant than maize.

points.description: Absorbs water from a larger volume of soil.
Waxy bloom on leaves / leaves roll in dry weather (or can become dormant in drought).
Reduces water loss by transpiration (or recovers growth when rain returns).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sorghum has an extensive fibrous root system, so it takes up water from a large volume of soil. Its leaves have a waxy bloom and roll up in heat, which reduces water loss by transpiration.

explanation: Feature plus how it helps.
hints: Give a feature and say how it saves or gets water.

stem: Suggest **three** ways a farmer near Masvingo could reduce bird damage to a sorghum crop.

points.description: Plant early and at the same time as neighbours so the crop does not ripen alone.
Scare birds (people, noise, scarecrows, reflective strips) during grain filling and harvest promptly when ripe.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She could grow a brown high-tannin sorghum, plant at the same time as her neighbours so many fields ripen together, and scare birds from the soft-dough stage, then harvest as soon as the grain is hard.

explanation: Cultivar, timing, scaring, prompt harvest.
hints: Think of cultivar, timing and protection.

stem:
A farmer near Gwanda grew three cereals side by side in a season with a long dry spell in February.

| Crop | Grain yield (t/ha) |
| --- | --- |
| Maize (early hybrid) | 1.2 |
| Sorghum | 2.1 |
| Pearl millet | 1.8 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage by which the sorghum yield exceeded the maize yield.
parts.explanation: (2.1 − 1.2) ÷ 1.2 × 100 = 75.00000000000001%. Dividing by the sorghum yield instead gives 42.9%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. (2.1 − 1.2) ÷ 1.2 × 100 = 75.00000000000001%. Dividing by the sorghum yield instead gives 42.9%.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which crop was most affected by the dry spell?

options.content: Sorghum
options.rationale: Sorghum gave the highest yield.

options.content: Pearl millet
options.rationale: Pearl millet gave 1.8 t/ha, more than maize.

options.content: Maize (early hybrid)
options.rationale: Correct: it gave the lowest yield, 1.2 t/ha.

options.content: All were affected equally
options.rationale: The yields differ widely.

parts.explanation: Maize, which is most sensitive to drought at flowering, yielded least.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why maize yield falls sharply when a dry spell occurs at tasselling and silking.

points.description: Water stress at flowering delays silking / dries the silks and pollen.
So fewer kernels are fertilised and cobs are small or barren.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** reasons why the farmer might still grow some maize despite these results.

points.description: Maize is the preferred staple food of the family.
Maize has a ready market (e.g. the GMB or local buyers) and is easier to process (milling).
In seasons with good rain maize yields more; it suffers less bird damage than small grains.

parts.explanation: Food preference, markets, bird damage, good-season yields.

explanation: Interpret a dry-season trial and explain the choice of cereals.

stem: Rudo plans to grow 4 ha of wheat near Marondera. She will apply a compound fertiliser containing 7% N at 400 kg/ha before planting and ammonium nitrate (34.5% N) at 250 kg/ha as top dressing. Each irrigation applies 35 mm of water. Fertiliser is sold in 50 kg bags.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bags of the compound fertiliser needed. Round UP to whole bags.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total mass of nitrogen applied per hectare, in kg, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of water applied to the whole field in one irrigation, in m³.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: At which stage should Rudo stop irrigating the wheat?

options.content: At tillering
options.rationale: Tillering needs water to form many tillers.

options.content: At flowering
options.rationale: Water stress at flowering reduces grain set.

options.content: Straight after the nitrogen top dressing
options.rationale: Top dressing must be watered in.

options.content: When the grain has filled and is hardening
options.rationale: Correct: water is no longer needed and would delay harvest.

parts.explanation: Irrigation continues through grain filling and stops as the grain hardens and dries.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why Rudo should plant by about May and not delay until July.

points.description: Late wheat fills its grain in hot weather (September-October), which shortens grain filling and lowers yield.
Late wheat may still be in the field when the rains start, so the grain sprouts or is damaged and harvest is difficult.

parts.explanation: Heat at grain fill; rain at harvest.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe how the seedbed for wheat should be prepared, giving reasons.

points.description: Plough or disc to bury residues and weeds.
Harrow to a fine, firm tilth so the small seed has good contact with moist soil.
Level the land so that irrigation water spreads evenly without ponding or dry patches.

explanation: Fertiliser, nitrogen and irrigation calculations for wheat, and timing and seedbed reasons.

stem: Thandeka drills sorghum in rows 80 cm apart and thins it to 10 cm in the row. A germination test shows 75% germination. 1,000 seeds have a mass of 30 g.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the plant population per hectare.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the minimum mass of seed needed per hectare, in kg.
parts.explanation: Seeds = 125,000 ÷ 0.75 = 166,667; × 0.03 g = 5,000 g = 4.999999999999999 kg/ha. Ignoring germination gives 3.75 kg; multiplying by 0.75 gives 2.81 kg.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Seeds = 125,000 ÷ 0.75 = 166,667; × 0.03 g = 5,000 g = 4.999999999999999 kg/ha. Ignoring germination gives 3.75 kg; multiplying by 0.75 gives 2.81 kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why small-grain seed needs a fine, firm seedbed.

points.description: The seed is small, so it must be sown shallowly and needs close contact with moist soil to absorb water.
Large clods leave air spaces where the seed dries out, and seedlings cannot push through a crust or clods.

explanation: Population and seed rate for sorghum, and seedbed needs of small seeds.
